query: Earlier studies on stainless, alloy, and boiler steels reported improved hardness, wear resistance, thermal stability, or reduced mass change during aggressive salt exposure at 700–900 °C. However, these findings were specific to individual material systems and emphasized characterization or performance rather than establishing why corrosion protection persists or fails across room- and high-temperature regimes; studies combining HEAs, subsequent annealing, and hot-corrosion assessment were also reported to be minimal. For Q235 steel in its pre-exposure state, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain its corrosion-related degradation or retention of protection under these regimes? Specify a controlled study that would isolate the governing cause, predicted observations relative to an appropriate reference, the conditions under which the hypothesis should and should not apply, supporting evidence from the earlier studies, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In Q235 steel in its pre-exposure state, high-temperature exposure (700–900°C) to an aggressive salt environment promotes the formation of a protective oxide layer that governs its corrosion resistance. When this oxide layer remains stable and adherent, corrosion is mitigated; conversely, if the layer is unstable or spalls, accelerated corrosion occurs.
generation.material_initial_state: Q235 steel in its pre-exposure state with its native microstructure
generation.intervention: Expose Q235 steel samples to an aggressive salt environment at high temperatures (700–900°C)
generation.conditions: Exposure under a controlled aggressive salt environment at high temperatures, with comparisons made to baseline conditions such as room temperature or non-salt environments
generation.structural_mediator: Formation and stability of a protective oxide layer on the surface of Q235 steel
generation.mechanism: High-temperature salt exposure induces an oxide layer that serves as a barrier to further corrosion. If the oxide is stable and adherent, it reduces the rate of degradation; if the oxide becomes unstable or spalls, fresh metal is exposed to corrosive attack, accelerating degradation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples that form a stable, adherent oxide layer will exhibit lower mass loss and maintain mechanical properties like hardness compared to samples where the oxide layer is unstable or absent, which will show increased corrosion damage.
generation.baseline: Q235 steel samples maintained at room temperature or in non-salt environments, where minimal oxidation and corrosion are expected.
generation.boundary: This protective mechanism is expected to be significant only under high-temperature aggressive salt conditions (700–900°C) and may not apply at lower temperatures or with different corrosive agents.
generation.uncertainty: The exact temperature threshold and environmental parameters at which the protective oxide layer shifts from stable to unstable are not fully defined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Q235 steel samples with identical initial conditions. Expose one set to an aggressive salt environment at 700–900°C for a fixed duration while keeping a control set at room temperature or in a non-salt environment. After exposure, assess the formation, uniformity, and adherence of the oxide layer using microscopy and diffraction techniques, and evaluate corrosion-related properties by measuring mass change and hardness.
measurements: Mass change before and after exposure
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the high-temperature salt-exposed samples do not show a correlation between the stability/adherence of the oxide layer and improved corrosion resistance (i.e., they do not maintain lower mass change or hardness degradation relative to the baseline), or if no significant oxide formation differences are observed between samples, the hypothesis will be falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: A pre‐exposure annealing treatment on Q235 steel promotes the formation of a uniform, adherent duplex oxide scale that acts as a diffusion barrier during high-temperature aggressive salt exposure (700–900 °C), thus reducing corrosion-related degradation compared to untreated steel. In contrast, in its as-received state, Q235 steel develops a less uniform oxide layer that inadequately protects against rapid corrosion at high temperatures.
drafts.material_initial_state: Untreated Q235 steel with its normal microstructure and inclusions as found in standard industrial applications.
drafts.intervention: A controlled pre‐exposure annealing treatment, designed to facilitate the formation of a uniform protective oxide layer.
drafts.conditions: Samples will be exposed to both room temperature and high-temperature (700–900 °C) environments in the presence of an aggressive salt (e.g., Na2SO4 or similar), to distinguish baseline corrosion behavior from high-temperature effects.
drafts.structural_mediator: The duplex oxide scale that forms during annealing, likely consisting of an inner stable Fe3O4 (magnetite) layer coupled with an outer less stable oxide, whose uniformity and adhesion are critical for reducing oxygen and ion diffusion.
drafts.mechanism: Pre-annealing enables the controlled formation of a protective oxide scale with improved uniformity and adhesion; this scale acts as a barrier to further oxidation and salt-induced corrosion at high temperatures. Without the annealing, the oxide growth is non-uniform and less protective, leading to accelerated corrosion and increased mass change during salt exposure.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Under high-temperature aggressive salt conditions, pre-annealed Q235 steel will display lower mass change, reduced microstructural degradation, and better retention of mechanical properties compared to untreated steel. At room temperature, differences are predicted to be minimal due to slower kinetics of oxidation and corrosion.
drafts.baseline: Untreated (as-received) Q235 steel, which is expected to form an irregular oxide layer that offers inferior protection under high-temperature, salt-exposure conditions.
drafts.boundary: The hypothesized protective mechanism via an annealing-induced oxide scale is expected to be significant only in high-temperature corrosion environments (700–900 °C) with aggressive salt exposure; at room temperature, the differences in oxidation behavior may be too subtle to yield significant performance differences.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Q235 steel samples. One set undergoes a controlled pre‐exposure annealing treatment and the other remains untreated. Expose both sets to an aggressive salt environment at high temperatures (700–900 °C) and as a separate condition at room temperature. Evaluate mass change, oxide scale uniformity (using SEM/EDS), phase composition (via XRD), and hardness/wear resistance.
measurements: Microstructural analysis (SEM/EDS) to assess oxide uniformity and scale thickness
Phase identification (via XRD) of oxide layers
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not exhibit statistically significant improvements in corrosion resistance (i.e., lower mass change, more uniform and adherent oxide layer, and better mechanical properties) compared to untreated samples in the high-temperature salt exposure tests, or if similar levels of protection are observed at both temperatures, then the hypothesis would be falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: A protective iron oxide layer initially forms on Q235 steel in salt-containing environments at moderate high temperatures (around 700 °C), but it becomes unstable and spalls at higher temperatures (above ~800 °C), leading to increased corrosion as fresh metal is exposed.
drafts.material_initial_state: As-received or as-rolled Q235 steel with any native surface oxide scale removed prior to testing.
drafts.intervention: Expose Q235 steel samples directly to a controlled salt environment (e.g., Na2SO4-laden environment) at multiple temperatures (700, 800, and 900 °C), with or without an intermediate annealing step, for fixed durations to foster oxide scale formation and potential degradation.
drafts.conditions: Salt exposure in a furnace under static air at incremental temperatures (up to 900 °C) for comparable durations (e.g., 24–72 hours), with controlled salt application (consistent mass/area) to ensure reproducible deposition.
drafts.structural_mediator: An initially protective iron oxide scale whose breakdown kinetics change with temperature, microstructure evolution, and salt-induced chemical reactions.
drafts.mechanism: At moderate temperatures, a stable oxide scale impedes corrosive species from reaching the steel substrate. Above a threshold temperature near 800 °C, the oxide scale experiences spallation and accelerated chemical attack, exposing reactive iron surface to further corrosive damage.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Compared to a low-temperature or non-salt-exposed baseline, Q235 steel will retain a relatively slow corrosion rate at 700 °C due to a continuous oxide film, but show significantly higher mass loss and deeper pitting at 900 °C as the oxide film breaks down.
drafts.baseline: A reference set of Q235 steel samples tested without salt exposure or at lower temperatures (<600 °C) to confirm minimal or standard oxidation behavior.
drafts.boundary: Below ~600 °C, salt-induced corrosion is limited, so the hypothesis does not strongly apply. Above ~900 °C or under different aggressive chemistries (e.g., chlorides), scale behavior and corrosion modes could differ markedly, potentially invalidating the mechanism.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare Q235 samples with identical surface finishes, apply uniform salt deposits, then expose them at different temperatures (e.g., 600, 700, 800, and 900 °C) for fixed durations. Perform mass-change measurements before and after exposure, followed by cross-sectional microstructural, SEM/EDS, and XRD analyses on the oxide scale.
measurements: Thickness, composition, and morphology of oxide scales (SEM, EDS, cross sections)
Depth of corrosion penetration or pitting
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If Q235 steel remains uniformly protected without scale breakdown or spallation above ~800 °C, or if no protective scale is observed at ~700 °C, the hypothesis is disproven.

drafts.hypothesis: The corrosion-related degradation or retention of protection in Q235 steel under aggressive salt exposure at 700–900 °C is governed by the formation and stability of a protective oxide layer, which is influenced by the steel's microstructure and the presence of alloying elements. Annealing treatments that refine grain size and promote the formation of stable, adherent oxides will enhance corrosion resistance, while coarse-grained or non-uniform microstructures will lead to accelerated degradation due to non-uniform oxide growth and spallation.
drafts.material_initial_state: Q235 steel in its pre-exposure state, with a typical microstructure for as-received or untreated material.
drafts.intervention: Apply annealing treatments to Q235 steel to vary grain size and microstructural uniformity, followed by exposure to aggressive salt environments at 700–900 °C.
drafts.conditions: Aggressive salt exposure at 700–900 °C, with controlled variations in annealing temperature and time to produce different microstructures.
drafts.structural_mediator: The grain size and uniformity of the microstructure, which influence the formation and stability of the protective oxide layer.
drafts.mechanism: Annealing treatments modify the microstructure of Q235 steel, affecting the nucleation and growth of protective oxide layers during high-temperature salt exposure. Fine, uniform grains promote the formation of a stable and adherent oxide layer, while coarse or non-uniform grains lead to non-uniform oxide growth, increased spallation, and accelerated corrosion.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Annealed Q235 steel with fine, uniform grains will exhibit reduced mass loss and improved thermal stability compared to as-received or coarsely grained samples under identical salt exposure conditions.
drafts.baseline: As-received Q235 steel without annealing treatment, exposed to the same aggressive salt conditions.
drafts.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold for Q235 steel exposed to aggressive salt environments at 700–900 °C but may not apply to other temperature ranges or environments with different corrosive agents.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare Q235 steel samples with varying microstructures through controlled annealing treatments. Expose these samples, along with as-received Q235 steel as a reference, to aggressive salt environments at 700 °C, 800 °C, and 900 °C for a fixed duration. Measure mass change, oxide layer composition, and adhesion properties.
measurements: Mass change of samples after exposure
Oxide layer composition using X-ray diffraction (XRD)
Oxide layer adhesion using scratch testing
Microstructural analysis using scanning electron microscopy (SEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If annealed Q235 steel with fine, uniform grains does not exhibit significantly reduced mass loss or improved oxide layer stability compared to as-received or coarsely grained samples under identical conditions, the hypothesis will be falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Q235 steel exhibits reduced corrosion degradation when subjected to high-temperature exposure (700–900 °C) due to the formation of a protective oxide layer that enhances thermal stability and wear resistance.
drafts.material_initial_state: Q235 steel in its pre-exposure state, unexposed to high temperatures or aggressive salt environments.
drafts.intervention: Expose Q235 steel samples to high temperatures (700–900 °C) in a salt environment for a defined period.
drafts.conditions: The hypothesis should apply under high-temperature exposure in a corrosive salt environment. It may not apply under low-temperature conditions or in non-corrosive environments.
drafts.structural_mediator: Formation of a protective oxide layer on the surface of Q235 steel.
drafts.mechanism: At high temperatures, Q235 steel reacts with the salt environment to form a stable oxide layer that mitigates further corrosion and enhances material properties.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Samples of Q235 steel exposed to high temperatures in a salt environment will show less mass loss and improved hardness compared to unexposed samples or those exposed to lower temperatures.
drafts.baseline: Q235 steel samples that have not been exposed to high temperatures or corrosive environments.
drafts.boundary: The hypothesis may not hold true for other steel grades or under different environmental conditions (e.g., non-salt environments or temperatures below 700 °C).

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct a controlled experiment comparing Q235 steel samples exposed to high temperatures in a salt environment against a control group at room temperature and in a non-corrosive environment.
measurements: microstructural analysis of the oxide layer
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the high-temperature exposed samples do not show significantly less mass loss or improved hardness compared to the control samples, the hypothesis will be falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: The formation of a stable, adherent oxide layer on Q235 steel, composed of iron, silicon, and manganese oxides, contributes to its corrosion protection under room- and high-temperature regimes.
drafts.material_initial_state: Q235 steel in its pre-exposure state
drafts.mechanism: Thermally grown oxide layer formation and stability
drafts.predicted_outcome: Improved hardness, wear resistance, thermal stability, or reduced mass change during aggressive salt exposure
drafts.baseline: Q235 steel without exposure to aggressive salt
drafts.boundary: Temperature range of 700-900 °C and exposure to aggressive salt

falsification_experiment.design: Controlled exposure of Q235 steel to aggressive salt at 700-900 °C, with and without pre-treatment to enhance or disrupt oxide layer formation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-treatment does not result in a significant difference in corrosion-related degradation or retention of protection, the hypothesis is falsified
